issues.body: `_marker_index` accepts a marker from every issue body and `verify_migration` then uses any unique match as the authoritative bd-id mapping. Issue bodies are forgeable by unprivileged users; this file's existing resume path explicitly authenticates mappings with `bd-migration`, checkpoint provenance, or a trusted author/title contract. A decoy can therefore satisfy a missing mapping (and, if its body contains the expected edge text, make an incomplete migration verify clean), or create a duplicate that permanently fails verification. Merely saying verification must see duplicates does not make an untrusted marker authoritative.
issues.fix_hint: Build the authoritative verification map from migration-owned provenance (at minimum the authenticated migration label, with the established legacy/checkpoint rules as needed), while reporting unauthenticated marker collisions separately. Add a test where an unprivileged/unlabelled decoy is the sole marker and prove it cannot make verification succeed.
issues.title: Verification treats unauthenticated bd-id markers as migrated issues

issues.body: `_marker_present(body, "Blocked-by: #2")` returns true for `Blocked-by: #20` (and similarly for parent markers), so the verifier can report a clean migration while the dependent points at a different blocker. The new wrong-target test uses `#9999` versus `#2640`, which does not exercise this prefix collision. Sharing the predicate with the writer makes behavior consistent but does not make it correct.
issues.fix_hint: Match a complete marker line/token with an issue-number boundary, such as an escaped regex anchored to line boundaries or `(?![0-9])`, and use that exact predicate in both writer and verifier. Add tests for expected `#2` with bodies containing `#20`, `#21`, and the exact `#2` marker.
issues.title: Substring matching accepts an edge to the wrong issue number

verdict.summary: The new verifier can both trust attacker-controlled issue markers and accept a dependency marker for the wrong issue number. Those flaws undermine its core promise of reliably reconciling the completed migration. The added self-tests cover duplicates and a clearly different target, but not either adversarial/proximity case.
